question: Can a label-free measure of prediction invariance serve as a reliable proxy for model accuracy across architectures and test distributions?

key_findings.claim: Effective invariance (EI) jointly encodes prediction consistency and confidence for an image and its transformed counterpart.
key_findings.evidence: EI is the geometric mean of the two top-class confidences when the predicted classes agree and zero otherwise, avoiding Jensen-Shannon cases that rate two low-confidence or different-argmax predictions as highly invariant.

key_findings.claim: Across a large controlled model collection, rotation and grayscale EI are strongly correlated with both in- and out-of-distribution accuracy.
key_findings.evidence: The study evaluates 150 ImageNet classifiers over eight test sets; rotation gives model-centric Pearson r above 0.915 and Spearman rho above 0.875, grayscale gives r above 0.84 and rho above 0.82, and dataset-centric ImageNet-C correlations for three models exceed r=0.93 and rho=0.95.

key_findings.claim: The relationship is descriptive and subgroup-sensitive rather than a causal or universal accuracy estimator.
key_findings.evidence: Within hard-test subsets or standard-training groups, rank correlation can weaken; augmentation-trained models deviate on ImageNet-A, and models trained on more real data form distinct trends. EI also includes confidence, itself already related to accuracy.

method.core_idea: Measure how confidently a classifier preserves its top prediction under simple label-preserving transformations, then test whether that unlabeled statistic tracks accuracy.
method.mechanism: Compute predictions on original and 90/180/270-degree rotations or grayscale images, average confidence-weighted agreement into EI, and regress EI against labeled accuracy across model-centric and dataset-centric panels with Pearson, Spearman, robust regression, and bootstrap analysis.
assumptions: The selected transformations should preserve the semantic label for the evaluated dataset.
Model confidence is sufficiently comparable across architectures and training recipes.
The evaluated model/dataset panel represents the deployment variation for which EI will be used.

techniques.role: Combines top-class agreement with paired prediction confidence without labels.
Compares many architectures and training strategies on fixed test sets.
Compares each fixed model across natural and synthetic shifts.

evaluations.setting: 150 ImageNet classifiers spanning convolutional networks, transformers, augmentation, and extra-data training across eight ID/OOD sets, plus CIFAR-10 analyses.
evaluations.metric: EI, Jensen-Shannon divergence, test accuracy, Pearson r, Spearman rho, robust linear fit, and 1,000-sample bootstrap uncertainty.
evaluations.result: EI has consistently high aggregate accuracy correlation and outperforms JS as an invariance proxy, with notable subgroup and hard-shift deviations that limit universal model selection.
evaluations.baseline: Jensen-Shannon prediction divergence, accuracy-drop invariance, and accuracy-on-the-line style ID/OOD correlations.

limitations: Only image classification and two hand-selected transformations are studied.
EI conflates invariance with calibration/confidence, so it is not a pure transformation-consistency statistic.
Aggregate correlations can be driven by architecture, pretraining-data, or training-recipe groups and need not hold within a candidate subset.
The study uses unlabeled target inputs but does not validate prospective model selection under previously unseen shifts.
failure_modes: A label-changing transformation makes high sensitivity desirable and invalidates EI.
Miscalibrated overconfidence inflates EI without commensurate accuracy.
Models exploit a transformation-specific shortcut that has no connection to deployment robustness.
Noise, nuisance features, or spurious correlations invert or shatter the fitted accuracy relationship.
reusable_insights: A proxy intended for model selection must be evaluated within the actual candidate-model subgroup, not only across a heterogeneous leaderboard.
Confidence-weighted consistency can repair simple divergence-metric pathologies but introduces calibration dependence.
Prospective validation should include transformations, shifts, and nuisance conditions deliberately chosen to break the hypothesized line.
open_questions: Which automatically discovered transformations yield complementary rather than redundant accuracy signals?
Can calibration-normalized or class-conditional EI retain correlation within narrow model families?
How should uncertainty and subgroup shift be propagated when EI predicts an unlabeled target accuracy?

competitive_landscape.title: Accuracy on the Line: On the Strong Correlation Between Out-of-Distribution and In-Distribution Generalization
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest large-scale correlation phenomenon for ID and OOD accuracy.
competitive_landscape.difference: Accuracy-on-the-line relates two labeled accuracies; the target substitutes a label-free confidence-weighted invariance statistic and studies both model- and dataset-centric views.

competitive_landscape.title: Measuring Robustness to Natural Distribution Shifts in Image Classification
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational broad ImageNet shift testbed and robustness comparison.
competitive_landscape.difference: Taori et al. show synthetic robustness often fails to transfer to natural shifts and emphasize diverse real training data; the target proposes a transformation statistic that correlates with accuracy but does not establish robustness transfer causally.

competitive_landscape.title: Accuracy on the wrong line: On the pitfalls of noisy data for out-of-distribution generalisation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later primary counterexample to correlation-based OOD prediction.
competitive_landscape.difference: It proves and demonstrates that noise, nuisance dimensions, and shortcuts can make ID/OOD accuracies negatively correlated, sharpening the target paper's subgroup caveats and motivating adversarial validation of EI lines.

novelty_assessment: EI is a simple, useful label-free proxy whose confidence-and-consistency construction fixes concrete divergence failures, and the 150-model panel is substantial. The central evidence remains correlation over selected transformations and panels; later wrong-line results underscore that deployment requires subgroup-specific and stress-tested calibration.
reviewer_notes: Read all 18 extracted pages, including the EI definition, correlation tables, subgroup analyses, and appendices. Primary robustness and later counterexample records were checked on arXiv/PMLR on 2026-08-23.
